To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the ingestion of protein and AAs is associated with increased MPS in human skeletal muscle; 2) leucine, the branched chain AA with the highest plasma concentration, is the most potent AA for stimulating MPS; 3) the rate and magnitude of MPS responses are highly dependent on the type and quantity of protein ingested; and 4) MPS is impaired in elderly individuals, which may reflect a combination of age related reductions in muscle protein synthesis and/or increased protein breakdown

the anabolic effects of protein/AAs are influenced by 1) the source of protein/AAs, with milk protein/AAs being most effective; 2) the time of day, with the greatest anabolic effects occurring in the morning; and 3) the timing and frequency of protein/AAs relative to exercise, with the most effective timing occurring immediately after exercise.
the ingestion of dietary proteins or AAs stimulates MPS and that this response is modulated by the source of protein, the amount and type of AA, and the age and gender of the individual.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the body responds to dietary AAs and the mechanisms by which they regulate skeletal muscle protein turnover.
understanding the molecular mechanisms by which AAs regulate skeletal muscle protein metabolism and how these mechanisms are affected by aging and disease states.
the mechanisms by which AAs regulate muscle protein turnover and how these responses are affected by aging.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AAs are essential for muscle growth, maintenance, and regeneration.
the ingestion of protein/AA-rich foods or supplements stimulates MPS, and that these responses are influenced by the type and amount of protein consumed.
the ingestion of protein/AA mixtures, especially those containing leucine, is an effective means to promote muscle protein synthesis and muscle hypertrophy in both younger and older individuals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

protein/AAs, particularly leucine, are potent stimulants of muscle protein synthesis, but the magnitude of this response is modulated by the type of protein/AAs ingested and the age of the individual.
AAs are important for maintaining skeletal muscle protein homeostasis and that the anabolic response to protein/AA nutrition is highly sensitive to the type, dose and frequency of ingestion.

AAs play a central role in the regulation of human skeletal muscle proteostasis, and that a better understanding of the mechanisms by which AAs modulate muscle protein metabolism will lead to the development of effective nutritional interventions for the prevention and treatment of age-associated sarcopenia.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the human skeletal muscle proteome is highly dynamic and responsive to dietary protein/AA intake, and that the magnitude of these responses is influenced by the source of the protein and the AA content, as well as the time of day.
AAs are important modulators of human muscle protein metabolism.

the human body is remarkably adept at maintaining muscle homeostasis, and that the body has a robust ability to adapt to the intake of different protein sources, and to respond to the intake of specific AAs.
